analysis.one_liner: Directs the Energy Department to help states and industry cut methane wasted by flaring and venting at oil and gas sites.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: it was referred to two House committees in October 2023, sent to a subcommittee, and died with no cosponsors and no vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Energy to run a program to reduce methane emissions from flaring and venting during oil and gas production. It is a voluntary, cooperative approach: the Energy Department would give technical help to states and industry, speed up technologies for capturing gas instead of burning it off, keep a database of state flaring rules, and report back to Congress on barriers to capturing the gas. It stresses that states remain the main regulators and imposes no mandates or penalties on producers.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near oil and gas production, who breathe fewer harmful air pollutants, and everyone affected by climate change, since methane is a potent greenhouse gas. Oil and gas producers also benefit if they can capture and sell gas that would otherwise be flared or vented as waste.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near oil and gas fields

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Energy Department to carry out a comprehensive program to reduce methane emissions from flaring and venting during oil and natural gas production [S2].

Directs the department to provide technical assistance to state regulators, utilities, industry, and tribal and local stakeholders, and to accelerate technologies and practices that reduce flaring and venting [S3].

Requires a report to Congress, within 270 days of enactment, on existing flaring and venting rules, technology initiatives, and barriers to commercially capturing gas that would otherwise be wasted [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the Energy Department program, and oil and gas companies would face costs if they chose to adopt capture technologies, though the bill offers assistance rather than requirements and captured gas can be sold.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates no binding limits on flaring or venting and explicitly recognizes states as the primary regulators, so polluters would face no new federal mandate; results would depend entirely on voluntary state and industry action [S3].
The bill authorizes no funding and sets no emission-reduction target, so its real-world effect would likely be limited to reports, databases, and convening [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's aim — cutting methane, a potent greenhouse gas that also harms local air quality — is broadly beneficial, and capturing wasted gas can pay for itself. But its design is deliberately light: voluntary assistance, no mandates, no targets, and no funding. Even if enacted, its impact on emissions would likely be modest compared with binding flaring rules.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees in October 2023 and then to a subcommittee, where it sat; it never got a markup, a floor vote, or any cosponsors, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Curtis introduced the bill in the House on October 17, 2023 [S1].
On October 25, 2023, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Science, Space, and Technology Committee [S5].
On November 3, 2023, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials [S5].
No further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died in committee without a vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers are no worse off and gained nothing — no mandates were ever enacted, and no federal flaring program was created. The bill was so modest that its death changed little for anyone.

for.name: Rep. John R. Curtis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and offered it for consideration; it was referred to committee.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, assigned it to its Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials Subcommittee, and never brought it to a markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so its level of support in both parties was never tested; the sole sponsor was a Republican.

industries.note: The bill would have required nothing of producers, only offering technical help to capture and sell gas now flared or vented, so most of the industry had little to lose and something to gain. Producers operating near communities also face air-quality and liability pressure from wasted-gas emissions, which voluntary capture could ease.
